headline: Sow cover crops and your last cold-hardy greens now — the fall planting window closes within days.

tasks.title: Cover crops & last greens
tasks.detail: Sow winter rye or oats over empty beds to protect and feed the soil over winter. You can still direct-sow spinach, arugula, and mâche for an overwintered spring crop if you tuck them under row cover.

tasks.title: Frost watch — keep covers handy
tasks.detail: First frost can reach the Seacoast from late September into mid-October. Keep row cover or old bedsheets ready to throw over tomatoes, peppers, and basil on clear, still nights near or below freezing.

tasks.title: Winter squash & tender crops
tasks.detail: Pick and cure winter squash and pumpkins before frost, and keep harvesting tomatoes, beans, and peppers. Any green tomatoes will finish ripening indoors on a warm windowsill.

tasks.title: Garlic bed & spring bulbs
tasks.detail: Work compost into a bed now for garlic, which goes in mid-October to early November. This is also prime time to start planting daffodil and tulip bulbs for spring.

tasks.title: Deep fall watering
tasks.detail: Fall spells can be dry. Water perennials, shrubs, and any new fall plantings deeply so their roots head into winter well-hydrated — keep it up until the ground freezes.

tasks.title: Clean up disease
tasks.detail: Remove and trash — do not compost — any foliage showing late blight or powdery mildew. Clearing it now cuts down the spores that overwinter and hit next year's crop.
